opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting behavior, and I think there are a few things going on.

Part of it is just what the models learned from. So much of the code on the internet that's written in a conversational setting, like Stack Overflow answers, GitHub comments, or tutorials, has people writing "...rest of the code stays the same" or "// existing code here." Humans do that all the time because it's efficient. They're pointing at the part that matters. So the model picks up that habit as the natural way to talk about a code change.

There's also a training pressure toward brevity. If people rating responses prefer shorter, more focused answers, the model learns that rewriting four hundred lines to change one is worse. In a chat context that's often true. If I'm asking a quick question, I don't want a wall of text.

The problem shows up when you put that same model in an agentic setting, where its output gets written directly to a file. Then "rest of the function unchanged" isn't a helpful shorthand anymore. It's literally a bug. You've deleted half the file and replaced it with a comment. The model doesn't always have a strong sense of whether a human is reading its output or whether it goes straight into the filesystem.

That's a big reason we've leaned on tool design to fix it rather than just prompting. If you give the model a tool built around targeted edits, like "replace this exact string with this new string," the incentive to elide disappears. The model only has to write the part that's changing, which matches what it already wants to do, and you don't risk losing the unchanged code. Good tool design that works with the model's natural tendencies tends to beat fighting them with instructions like "always output the full file."

r001.rationale: The response points to internet examples such as Stack Overflow answers, GitHub comments, and tutorials where people use phrases like “rest of the code stays the same.”

r002.rationale: It says models may not distinguish a human-readable reply from output written directly to a file. It does not clearly say they cannot reliably infer whether the user wants only relevant changes or the entire code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favorite little quirks, because it's a pretty clean window into how these models actually learn. If you think about where the training data comes from, a huge chunk of it is humans talking about code with other humans. Stack Overflow answers, pull request comments, code review threads, GitHub issues. And when a human shows you a change, they almost never paste the whole file. They say "and then the rest stays the same" or they write a little "// ..." in the middle. That's just how people communicate about code efficiently.

So the model picks up that habit, and it's really a sensible habit in the human context. The problem is that the model doesn't fully understand the difference between explaining a change to a person and producing an artifact that's going to get written straight to disk. In the first case, eliding the unchanged parts is polite and helpful. In the second case, it's catastrophic, because now you've got a tool that takes "// rest of code unchanged" literally and deletes half your file.

There's also a laziness component, honestly, and I mean that somewhat literally. The model has been trained to be concise, to not waste the reader's time, and there's often RLHF pressure toward shorter outputs because people rate them higher. Reproducing four hundred lines of boilerplate verbatim is the opposite of that. So you get these two pressures pulling against each other: the user wants the whole file, but everything in the training signal says "don't pad your answer."

The way we think about fixing it is partly a training problem and partly a tooling problem. On the training side, you can teach the model to distinguish the two modes, and to be explicit about which one it's in. On the tooling side, this is a lot of why diff-based editing and search-and-replace style tools became popular. If you give the model a way to say "replace exactly this block with exactly that block," you sidestep the whole question. It doesn't have to choose between verbose and lossy, because it can express the change precisely and the harness does the rest. That ends up being better for everyone: fewer tokens, fewer accidental deletions, and it's actually closer to how a good engineer thinks about a change anyway.

r001.rationale: It says models learn from human code discussions, where people commonly show only changes and elide unchanged code.

r002.rationale: It describes difficulty distinguishing conversational explanations from file-writing artifacts, but does not clearly say models cannot reliably infer whether the user wants a partial change or the entire code.

astra-6.text: My guess is that a lot of the training data comes from people explaining code to other people. If you’re answering a question on Stack Overflow, you don’t copy the entire file—you show the part that changed and write something like, “The rest stays the same.” That’s helpful for a human reader, but if you’re taking the model’s output and writing it directly into a file, that omission becomes a bug. So there’s a mismatch between how people communicate code and what you need from a model that’s actually editing it.
